title: The People Sign a Binding Promise
overview: After confessing their past failures, the leaders and people of Jerusalem put their names to a written agreement to live by God's law and to support the temple.

parts.label: Leaders who signed (vv. 1-27)
parts.note: Nehemiah, the governor, signs first, then priests, Levites (temple assistants) and heads of the people, acting on behalf of everyone. Many names match family groups who had returned from exile in Babylon, so some may be clan names rather than single individuals, though scholars are not certain.

parts.label: Everyone joins the oath (vv. 28-29)
parts.note: The rest of the community, including wives and children old enough to understand, swear to follow the law given through Moses, calling a curse on themselves if they break it. The mention of people who set themselves apart from their neighbors for God's law may include outsiders who had joined Israel's faith, though readers differ on this.

parts.label: Marriage, rest days, debts (vv. 30-31)
parts.note: They promise not to marry into neighboring peoples, meant to protect their faith but also excluding outsiders, an issue that caused real pain elsewhere in this book and in Ezra. They also refuse to buy from traders on the Sabbath, the weekly rest day, and pledge every seventh year to leave fields unplanted and cancel debts, because poor families had been losing land to debt (chapter 5).

parts.label: A yearly temple tax (vv. 32-33)
parts.note: Each person would give a third of a shekel, a silver weight, each year to keep worship going: the bread placed before God, daily and festival offerings, and sacrifices to make things right between the people and God. The law of Moses mentions half a shekel, and it is unclear whether the smaller amount reflects poverty or a different weight standard.

parts.label: Wood, first crops, firstborn (vv. 34-36)
parts.note: Families drew lots to take turns supplying wood to keep the altar fire burning, and pledged the first part of each harvest as a gift to God. Firstborn sons were not sacrificed; under the law they were bought back with a payment, while firstborn animals went to the priests.

parts.label: Tithes and storerooms (vv. 37-39)
parts.note: A tenth of the crops would go to the Levites, who passed a tenth of that to the priests, with a priest present to keep the collection honest. It all ends with a summary promise to stay faithful to God's house, though chapter 13 shows the people later slipped on several of these points.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this signed pledge is mainly a model of wholehearted recommitment to God or mainly a sincere effort that, by later failing, shows the limits of trying to keep God's law through rules and promises.
think: What does putting a promise in writing and signing it in public add that a private intention does not, and why do even such promises sometimes fall apart?
